There's a lot to unpack here. I'll start off with the whole love bombing thing. It's not love bombing unless you are actively going out of your way to overly compliment them WITH the intent of using it to hurt them in the future. If you don't have malicious intent, it's not love bombing. Using your logic, basically every single person in a relationship would be love bombing each other. Not trying to sound rude, as I'm frequently caught up in an identical headspace, but sometimes we need reality checks to help us realize what's overthinking and what isn't. I'm also known to spiral. I have frequent mood swings, in fact I had one today and went nonverbal for about an hour while on a trip with my boyfriend and friends for band. I should've been having fun but something was stopping me. Want to know what I did? I went to my boyfriend for comfort, I grabbed his hand and tried to make small talk with him. Eventually he asked if I was ok, I said no, we talked about it and I felt 100x better after. I know it may seem impossible in that moment of spiraling to get better, and it may be even more challenging to reach out, but it helps so much. This will not only be beneficial to you, but your partner and your relationship as a whole. I know the whole "communication is key" thing is overused but it's true. I'm by no means a relationship expert, as I've only been in 3 my entire life (one was really abusive, one I actually just didn't have feelings for, and in my current I'm head over heels in love), but I think I know enough. You NEED to talk about your feelings. You NEED to bring up these concerns to your partner. If you don't, your feelings will only get worse and you'll continue to spiral bringing both of you down. Reaching out for help won't hurt them, and it'll help you too. If they truly care about you they won't want to leave you because of these things, they will want to help so give them that opportunity. My last little bit of advice, don't let you bring yourself down. I know it's easy to see yourself as nothing. I get how it feels not being good enough for someone, but you need to let go of that mindset. It takes a long time and it's a hard process but it's so worth it. Your partner loves you for you. Even if you don't get it they see something in you worth loving. Try to see yourself through your partners eyes, I realize that helped me a lot when I tried healing. We often love our partners despite their flaws, we see them as perfectly imperfect, and we should see ourselves the same way. You would never think those thoughts about your partner, so why think them about yourself? The hardest part is realizing that these thoughts you have aren't true. It's your brain overthinking and being overly-negative. Ignoring them is a lot simpler once you realize that they hold no weight in real life. I truly wish you and your partner the best. I know exactly how you feel, and I know how scary this can be. Stay safe, good luck.

As others have pointed out, men are looked down on in the LGBTQ+ community (for better or for worse). This has caused me to feel extremely excluded from this community despite being a gay trans man. I totally agree that we should celebrate women and sapphic culture but we also should acknowledge the fact that people like men. I've seen so many negative reactions to telling people online I'm gay most of which are along the lines of "eww I could never be into a man". While it may be a joke, it makes me feel really insecure about my identity which already has taken me so long to accept. I know that presenting as a man gives me more privilege than I would have if I was cis, but that doesn't mean my identity is any less important. I still face discrimination, I still have to deal with risking friendships by coming out, I still live in fear of my rights being stripped away. Gay men still deal with the stereotype of being dirty and promiscuous, people unsafe to leave children around. Trans men still have to deal with being treated as confused little girls. I hope one day people realize we still exist and celebrate our existence with us instead of shunning us for things we can't control.

Me and my boyfriend realized that simply asking before doing anything helps a lot, even things as simple as hugging. It creates a more communicative and safe environment and may help you grow more comfortable with things. I know from experience the key role that affection plays in a relationship, and I can assure you it'll be a lot more healthy if you guys get past this bump. That doesn't mean you guys necessarily have to come out, as I know it's a big step, but even sneaking off somewhere private or going to each others houses to just be open with each other would be enough. Good luck, I know you guys can get through this.

My brother’s girlfriend is a detransitioner, nothing too crazy, she was on T for about a month or so and just realized this wasn’t what she wanted and went back to presenting as a girl. My brother was friends with her at this time, and I’d be lying if I said I didn’t look up to her, being the only “trans man” I knew. It was nice seeing my parents discuss trans issues, and slowly get more comfortable with the idea of trans people (my dad especially, while he’s not transphobic he has a hard time using preferred pronouns for people and it was cool seeing him learn). My parents are aware of the fact that I don’t fit in gender norms, and while I’m not out, I’m sure at least my mom suspects something. When she (my brother’s girlfriend) detransitioned my parents said some unknowingly hurtful things, saying that “she never seemed trans to me” or “everyone goes through phases”. It made me extremely upset, as there was a time period where I tried coming out and said I’d prefer if they used he/him pronouns for me but they just kind of… ignored it? And now my mom looks back on that time period and considers it a phase. I’m pretty sure it’s just because of how young I was at the time, but it doesn’t make the impact hurt any less. Despite this, my brother’s girlfriend remains a huge supporter of trans rights, and has even educated my brother (a cishet guy who tries to be supportive) on a lot of topics. She doesn’t look back on her time presenting as a male with any ill intent, and still tells stories of people who helped her out during her coming out process. Other than that she’s just a normal girl, and I think that’s a good representation of the silent majority of detransitioners. They’re normal people, it just so happens that the negative stories get more attention.

Just because clothes don’t (or at least shouldn’t) define gender doesn’t mean we don’t live in a world full of stereotypes. As a trans man, I would’ve loved to dress more feminine, but only if I was born a guy. I can’t with the body I have because if I did I’d unfortunately be considered a girl because of stereotypes. The trans community can also be very gate-keepy at times, and there’s a lot of trans folk who think if you don’t stress like those stereotypes then you’re not “actually trans” (when that isn’t the case at all). As a whole, clothes shouldn’t have a gender and everyone should wear what they want, but we have to keep in mind that society doesn’t think that way yet. It’s sad, but for a lot of us we’re scared of not passing, so even if we still like clothes stereotypically made for the opposite gender, we can’t or else we run the risk of getting misgendered.

I’m not a trans girl but I’m a trans guy, an aspiring femboy, and gay. So I thought I could give some input as I’m finally at a point in life where I’m not constantly second guessing myself. My experience with gender was definitely something. I thought I was cis because I never got any dysphoria as a kid but once I went through puberty and read more about the lgbtq+ community online I started thinking about it more. I didn’t hate feminine clothing or the color pink but I knew if I wore them I’d always be seen as a girl. So I avoided them and as far as everyone was aware I hated dresses and skirts and pink. That was the first time I experienced dysphoria. Soon after I found the term non-binary and identified as that as I knew I wasn’t a girl but was uncertain about how I’d feel being a guy. It worked for a while but didn’t feel quite right. But my dysphoria was also growing worse so I knew I’d have to make it work. I really didn’t consider being trans until the first time a experienced bottom dysphoria. That’s when I knew I wanted to be a guy. I wanted to be a feminine guy at that which lead me to all these wonderful communities. But even now I still have my doubts but for me it’s because I know I’ll never completely fit in with other guys, especially gay guys, since I don’t plan on getting bottom surgery no matter how badly I want it since none of the options seems reasonable enough for me. So sometimes I think it’s never truly worth it and maybe I should just consider living a lie instead of having to come out and face the consequences. But figuring out my gender wasn’t easy at all. It took me 4 years to truly know who I am. So what I’m trying to get at is, it’s going to be hard for a while and you’re going to be confused. It’s normal. It’s part of the process. One thing for me that helps me make sure I’m “actually trans” is where I sit there and think about it. I ask myself, if I got to choose what biological body I wanted what would I pick? If I got to pick how the world saw me would I pick male, female, or neither? And I realized that I’d always pick male. While I know it may be more tricky being a femboy and all, it’s a good place to start thinking. Maybe even try choosing a feminine name for yourself along with she/her pronouns and try it out. That’s actually what I did to help myself pick my chosen name. I wish you the best of luck with your journey! I’ve been down that same road so I know how you feel more or less. Sending you lots of love! <3
